<reason>Side A built the stronger path to victory by consistently demonstrating that the 8:30 mandate produces conditional, uncertain sleep gains (due to bedtime shifting and long commutes) while imposing immediate, certain harms on elementary students, hourly workers, and underfunded districts. Side A effectively used the pressure questions to force Side B to defend specific failures of the universal floor, then answered Side B's pressure with disciplined A1/A2 structure that maintained the "certain cost versus uncertain benefit" asymmetry. Side B made strong biological arguments and clarified the floor-versus-ceiling distinction, but failed to fully neutralize the mechanism critique (bedtime shifting) or the distributional harm to younger children. Additionally, Side B's closing was clipped for exceeding the word limit, preventing full crystallization of their case and constituting a real execution cost.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>Side A's Rebuttal 2 decisively answered both pressure questions with proper A1/A2 structure, exposing that Side B's proposed fixes (flipped bus tiers, subsidized transport) transfer harm to elementary children without guaranteed funding, while maintaining that the mandate purchases only the "possibility" of sleep at the certain cost of family disruption and pre-dawn routes for younger students.</best_rebuttal>
